profile.name: Sardana de l'Alcalde
profile.tagline: A unique open-circle dance from Amer, Catalonia, where the mayor selects the music.
profile.insight: In the town of Amer, the Sardana de l'Alcalde is danced in an open circle that never closes, a unique tradition preserved since its 1949 revival following a decades-long political ban.
profile.profile: The Sardana de l'Alcalde is a traditional dance from Amer, Girona, characterized by its open-circle formation. Unlike standard sardanas, the dancers do not close the circle, a structural distinction that has persisted since the dance's 1949 revival. The tradition requires the town mayor to select the musical piece, a practice that has solidified the local repertoire over decades.
profile.profile_long:
The Sardana de l'Alcalde, or 'the Mayor's Sardana,' is a distinct cultural practice originating in the town of Amer, located in the La Selva region of Catalonia, Spain. While it shares many movement characteristics with the broader sardana tradition, it is distinguished by the fact that it is always danced in an open circle, never closing the loop. This structural choice serves as a defining feature of the dance, marking it as unique within the Catalan region. Oral histories trace the dance back to the late 19th century, with research by local expert and former mayor Josep Puigdemont suggesting its roots lie in the contrapàs, a forerunner to the sardana that emerged in the late 18th century.

The history of the dance is marked by a significant interruption. Around 1910, the tradition ceased due to intense political friction between the ruling party and the opposition. According to local memory, the enmity between these factions manifested during the dance, with couples from opposing sides booing one another, eventually leading to physical altercations. Consequently, the community deemed it appropriate to stop the performance entirely. This hiatus lasted until 1949, when the town celebrated the Millennium of the consecration of the Temple of Santa María, formerly the Monastery of the Order of Sant Benet. During these festivities, a document written by the town notary, Joan Porcioles, was discovered, providing a detailed account of the dance's ceremonial protocol. A local councilor, Narcís Solergastó, proposed reviving the dance based on these instructions, and the proposal was accepted.

A central component of the tradition is the mayor's role in selecting the musical piece. During the 1949 revival, the mayor, Narcís Junquera y Rigau, deferred the choice to councilor Salvador Oliveras i Galceran, who selected 'Conxita encisera' by Pere Mercader y Andrés. Later that year, the premiere of 'Fiesta milenaria' by local composer Joan Fontàs i Casas became a staple of the festival. Because Fontàs suffered from tuberculosis and relied on copyright royalties for his livelihood, the choice of his music became a matter of both tradition and community support. Mayor Junquera, who governed until 1975, consistently chose this piece, establishing a precedent that subsequent mayors have maintained. Today, the tradition remains active, with the repertoire unchanged, serving as a vital link to the town's civic and musical history.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated in Amer, Girona, with roots potentially tracing back to an 18th-century contrapàs. It was suppressed around 1910 due to political conflict and revived in 1949 during the Millennium celebrations of the Temple of Santa María.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in an open circle that never closes. Technique not described in sources beyond the open-circle formation.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is selected by the mayor. Central pieces include 'Conxita encisera' by Pere Mercader y Andrés and 'Fiesta milenaria' by Joan Fontàs i Casas.
sections.costume_and_setting: Traditionally performed during the town's main festival, historically on August 15, now held on the night of August 16 due to logistical reasons.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance serves as a civic tradition in Amer, symbolizing local identity and historical continuity. It is intrinsically linked to the role of the mayor, who holds the authority to select the music.
sections.notable_figures: Josep Puigdemont (researcher and former mayor), Narcís Solergastó (councilor who proposed revival), Narcís Junquera y Rigau (mayor who established the musical tradition), Joan Fontàs i Casas (composer), Pere Buxó i Domènech (musician who preserved the musical scores).
sections.regional_variants: The open-circle format is unique to the Sardana de l'Alcalde in Amer and is not found in other Catalan sardana traditions.
sections.lineage: A descendant of the contrapàs and a specific variant of the sardana.
